Indicated in chronic liver disease (high-risk group); standard dosing

summary: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23, 23-valent) provides active immunization against disease caused by the 23 Streptococcus pneumoniae capsular serotypes it contains, which account for most invasive pneumococcal disease. It is given as a single 0.5 mL intramuscular or subcutaneous dose. It is recommended for all adults 65 years and older and for persons 2 years and older at increased risk of pneumococcal disease (e.g., chronic heart, lung, liver, or kidney disease, diabetes, cigarette smoking, alcoholism, asplenia/sickle cell disease, cochlear implants, CSF leaks, and immunocompromising conditions). Because it is a pure polysaccharide vaccine, it does not produce a strong T-cell-dependent (memory/booster) response and is not effective in children under 2 years; pneumococcal conjugate vaccines are used in young children and are often given in sequence with PPSV23 in adults per current immunization schedules. A one-time revaccination after 5 years is recommended for certain high-risk and immunocompromised patients. It does not protect against serotypes not in the vaccine. Serious reactions are rare; local injection-site reactions are the most common adverse effects.
indications: Active immunization against pneumococcal disease caused by the 23 capsular serotypes in the vaccine
All adults 65 years of age and older

Persons 2 years and older at increased risk of pneumococcal disease (chronic cardiovascular, pulmonary, hepatic, or renal disease; diabetes mellitus; alcoholism; cigarette smoking; cerebrospinal fluid leak; cochlear implant)
Persons 2 years and older with functional or anatomic asplenia (including sickle cell disease) and immunocompromising conditions (e.g., HIV, malignancy, transplant, immunosuppressive therapy)

dosage.n: Coordinate timing with pneumococcal conjugate vaccine per current schedule

dosage.t: At least 5 years after the previous PPSV23 dose
dosage.n: For asplenia, immunocompromise, and those vaccinated before age 65 per recommendations

admin: Administer a single 0.5 mL dose by intramuscular or subcutaneous injection (do not give intradermally or intravenously)
Inspect for particulate matter/discoloration; do not mix in the same syringe with other vaccines (use separate sites)
Have epinephrine and supportive measures immediately available to treat anaphylaxis; observe the patient for syncope

moa: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine contains purified capsular polysaccharides from 23 serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae. After injection, these polysaccharide antigens stimulate the host's B lymphocytes to produce serotype-specific anticapsular antibodies (a largely T-cell-independent immune response). These antibodies promote opsonization, complement-mediated phagocytosis, and killing of pneumococci bearing the corresponding capsular types, providing protection against invasive disease caused by the included serotypes. Because the response is T-cell-independent, the vaccine does not reliably generate immunologic memory or robust booster responses and is poorly immunogenic in children younger than 2 years.

absolute: Severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to a previous dose of pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine or to any vaccine component
relative: Moderate or severe acute illness (defer until recovery)
Children younger than 2 years (poor immunogenicity; not indicated)
Recent or planned splenectomy/chemotherapy - time vaccination appropriately for optimal response
monitor: Appropriate scheduling relative to conjugate vaccine and any revaccination interval

preg: Safety during pregnancy has not been definitively established, and there is no evidence of harm; routine vaccination is generally deferred during pregnancy unless the woman is at high risk. When indicated for high-risk conditions, the potential benefit of protection against pneumococcal disease should be weighed against limited pregnancy data, ideally vaccinating before pregnancy where possible.
lact: It is not known whether vaccine components are excreted in human milk. The vaccine is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding, and breastfeeding is not a contraindication to maternal vaccination.
renal: Chronic renal failure and nephrotic syndrome are indications for vaccination because of increased pneumococcal disease risk; standard 0.5 mL dosing is used. Such patients are candidates for the recommended one-time revaccination after 5 years.
hepatic: Chronic liver disease (including cirrhosis) is an indication for vaccination; standard dosing applies. No hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

major: Immunosuppressive therapy (high-dose corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation, biologics) - may blunt the antibody response; vaccinate before immunosuppression where feasible
moderate: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) - administer in the recommended sequence/interval rather than simultaneously to optimize response
minor: Other inactivated vaccines may be given at the same visit using separate sites
interactions.alcohol: No interaction with alcohol; chronic alcoholism is itself an indication for vaccination.
interactions.diagnostics: No routine laboratory monitoring required; serologic confirmation of response is not generally needed.

common: Injection-site reactions - pain, erythema, swelling, induration
serious: Marked local reaction (extensive swelling of the injected limb), especially with revaccination too soon
rare: Guillain-Barre syndrome (reported rarely; causal relationship not established)
Thrombocytopenia in patients with stabilized idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (rare)
emergency: Anaphylaxis (difficulty breathing, throat/face swelling, hives, hypotension, collapse)

monitoring: Observe the patient after vaccination for immediate hypersensitivity reactions and syncope
Ensure correct scheduling relative to any pneumococcal conjugate vaccine and the 5-year revaccination interval where indicated
Document vaccination and high-risk indications for follow-up booster eligibility
counsel: This vaccine helps protect against serious pneumococcal infections like pneumonia, bloodstream infection, and meningitis caused by 23 common strains
Most people only need one dose; some at higher risk need a second dose at least 5 years later - your provider will advise
Soreness, redness, or swelling at the injection site and mild fever or aches are common and short-lived
It does not protect against every cause of pneumonia, and a separate conjugate vaccine may be recommended on a specific schedule
Tell your provider about any severe allergy to a previous dose, and report difficulty breathing, swelling, or hives right away
pk: Protective antibody levels generally develop within about 2-3 weeks of vaccination
Peak serotype-specific antibody response by ~3 weeks after the dose
Not applicable (vaccine - induces antibody response rather than drug levels)
Antibody levels decline over years; immunity is not lifelong, hence revaccination for selected high-risk groups
Refrigerate at 2-8 C (35-46 F); do not freeze; discard if frozen; protect per label
pearls: PPSV23 covers 23 capsular serotypes; recommended for ALL adults >=65 and for at-risk persons >=2 years (chronic heart/lung/liver/kidney disease, diabetes, smoking, alcoholism, asplenia/sickle cell, CSF leak, cochlear implant, immunocompromise)

Pure polysaccharide = T-cell-INDEPENDENT response - no strong immunologic memory/booster effect and ineffective under 2 years; conjugate vaccines (PCV) are used in young children and sequenced with PPSV23 in adults
A one-time revaccination after >=5 years is advised for certain high-risk/immunocompromised patients and those first vaccinated before age 65
Vaccinate at least 2 weeks BEFORE planned splenectomy or immunosuppression for best response where feasible
Does not protect against non-vaccine serotypes; follow current ACIP/national schedule for PCV-PPSV23 sequencing and intervals
missed: If a recommended dose is missed, administer it at the next opportunity - there is no need to restart a series. For high-risk patients due for the one-time revaccination, give it once at least 5 years after the prior dose; avoid revaccinating earlier than recommended because of increased local reactions.
overdose: Overdose is not a typical concern for a single-dose vaccine. Inadvertent administration of more than the recommended dose or earlier-than-recommended revaccination chiefly increases the likelihood and severity of local injection-site reactions. Management is supportive and symptomatic.
